August 29, 2011
PREFACE
The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) has developed a modular, multi-
user experimentation mini-facility for conducting droplet combustion science experiments in the
microgravity environment of the International Space Station (ISS). This facility, called the
Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA), resides in Combustion Integrated Rack
(CIR), a component of the Fluids and Combustion Facility (FCF) on-board the ISS. The
experiment FLEX-2 uses the FLEX platform to conduct droplet combustion tests, and requires
an on-orbit replacement radiometer that is sensitive at lower irradiance levels than the original
radiometer. This document describes the FLEX-2 calibration and characterization activities
necessary to satisfy science engineering requirements (sometimes also referred to as payload
performance requirements) contained in the FLEX-2 Engineering Requirements Document
(ERD), FLX-REQ-0001.

1.0 INTRODUCTION
1.1 Purpose
The purpose of this document is to report on the test results for calibration of the FLEX-2 Flight
Broadband and Narrowband Radiometers. Each Radiometer is calibrated independently in a
laboratory environment to provide accurate energy detection in a flight environment.
1.2 Scope
The scope of this report covers the test results from implementing the test plan MDC-TST-1866 from
June to August, 2011. Said tests calibrate and characterize the FLEX-2 Radiometers for flight.
Based on the results and observations from these tests, any procedural changes, deviations from the
plan, and results will be recorded in this final test report. This document does not cover all
verification test results.
1.3 Classification
The classification for the FLEX-2 Radiometer Package is Flight Model Development.
1.4 Order of Precedence for Verification Requirements
The verification requirements contained in this document shall take precedence over any conflicting
verification requirements.
1 Radiometer Calibration Test Report

3.2.1 Blackbody Infrared Source and Temperature Controller
The Blackbody IR Source from Infrared Systems Corporation consists of the Blackbody source and
temperature controller. Source temperature can be varied from 50 ºC to 1200 ºC, and source flux can
be varied by known amounts using the integrated Aperture Wheel.
3.2.2 DC Power Supply
The Power Supply used will provide ± 12 VDC power to the Radiometers. The specific
manufacturer, model, serial number, and calibration date are recorded and listed in Table I of this test
report.
3.2.3 Digital Voltmeter
The Digital Voltmeter will be used to measure the DC voltage output from each Radiometer for each
temperature data point. The specific manufacturer, model, serial number, and calibration date are
recorded and listed in Table I of this test report.
5 Radiometer Calibration Test Report

MDC-RPT-1881A
August 29, 2011
4.0 DESCRIPTION OF TEST ARTICLE & CONFIGURATION
The FLEX-2 Radiometer 2 (67235MFAC13950) consists of two independent Radiometers:
Broadband (BB) and Narrowband (NB). Each radiometer will be calibrated separately using the
same hardware setup and methods. By varying the blackbody source temperature and aperture size,
the irradiance values incident on the radiometer sensor head can be varied over a large range. By
recording the associated voltage output from each detector over the full range of blackbody
temperatures and aperture values, a family of calibration curves for each device can be constructed.
See APPENDIX H for further analysis to obtain irradiance values from the calibration. The ambient
temperature will be monitored via a calibrated laboratory temperature and humidity monitor. The
calibration process will be repeated for each radiometer in its preferred orientation.
4.1 Test Article
4.1.1 Radiometer Sub-Assembly
The Radiometer 2 (67235MFAC13950) consists of the broadband detector and the narrowband
detector (see FIGURE 4). The Radiometer 2 flight unit was assembled in-house at 6749 Engle Road.
4.1.1.1 Broadband Detector
The Broadband Detector is a COTS silicon-based thermopile detector from Dexter Research, Model
S60M with a KRS-5 (Thallium Bromo-Iodide) window (Dexter custom P/N DX-0916) providing
broadband transmission from 0.58 to 50 µm (see FIGURE 1 and 2). The range of flat spectral
response for the detector element is 100 nm to 100 µm, with an active area of 0.36 mm2. The back-
fill gas is Argon, and the aperture size is 0.125 inches. All other detector performance specifications
are satisfied in accordance to FLX-REQ-0001.
4.1.1.2 Narrowband Detector
The Narrowband Detector is a COTS thin film-based thermopile from Dexter Research; Model 2M
(Dexter custom P/N DX-0918). A combination of a Silicon Long Wave Pass (LWP) filter with a cut-
on wavelength of 5.0 µm and a Sapphire window that cuts off at ~ 7.0 µm is used to isolate the
desired spectral region of interest (~ 6.0 µm). The spectral scan of this combination is shown below
(FIGURE 3). The back-fill gas used is Xenon. The aperture size is 0.180 inches. All other detector
performance specifications are satisfied in accordance to FLX-REQ-0001.

4.2 Test Configuration
The Radiometer Sub-Assembly and the Blackbody Source is arranged on an optical bench. The
Blackbody Source output is aligned, via optical mounting hardware, with the opening of the
Radiometer Package (BB or NB) being tested. See FIGURE 5, FIGURE 6, and FIGURE 8. The
optical mounting hardware aligns and sets the horizontal distance from the detector input of the
Radiometer to the Blackbody aperture wheel, equal to the appropriate Flight distance of 110 mm.
FIGURE 5. FLEX-2 Radiometer & Blackbody Source Alignment.
10 Radiometer Calibration Test Report

MDC-RPT-1881A
August 29, 2011
The field of view measurements and response time measurements were made with the setup
configured as in FIGURE 5. However, during testing it was observed that the aperture wheel on the
blackbody source actually emitted radiation at significant levels compared to radiation from the
blackbody cavity. This extra radiation increasingly contributed to the total signal inversely
proportional to the aperture size, and had the systematic error of increasing the effective aperture size.
To reduce this error the blackbody calibration tests (only) were run with the setup shown in FIGURE
6. This modification added a low emissivity radiation shield between the radiometer and the
blackbody aperture wheel. The radiation shield has a few useful features:
1. Mounts on a slide, allowing the shield to be retracted away from the hot blackbody source
between measurements. By limiting the time resident near the hot blackbody source, the
temperature can be held at room temperature to within a few tenths of a degree Celsius.
2. The temperature of the radiation shield is monitored using a calibrated type K thermocouple,
accurate to one-tenth of a degree Fahrenheit.
3. The shield has a changeable aperture plate with highly repeatable positioning. A feature for
quick change-out of a selection of aperture plates allows measurements at different apertures
to be done quickly.
4. Low emissivity and high thermal mass keeps the shield’s temperature stable over longer
periods of time. Note: The narrowband radiometer is still sensitive to emissions at room
temperature.
5. The shield is mounted within 1 cm of the aperture wheel, and the shield apertures are the same
diameter as those in the aperture wheel; the aperture plates are also effectively thin (1.5 mm).
This arrangement allows the aperture wheel holes to still be the defining emitters in the
system, to first order.

5.0 TEST PROCEDURE
These procedures cover three characterizations of the FLEX-2 Radiometers:
i) Radiometric calibration,
ii) Field of View (FOV) roll-off measurement or instrument function, and
iii) Signal to Noise Ratios (SNR) of the radiometer subsystems.
5.1.1 Radiometer Calibration (performed separately on BB & NB)
The Radiometer Calibration Procedure is performed separately for each of the Broadband and
Narrowband Radiometers using the “Radiometer Calibration Procedure Datasheet” in APPENDIX B.
Within each of the Radiometer Calibration Procedures, specific data must be recorded for radiometer
voltage output over a range of apertures using a separate APPENDIX C, “Radiometer Calibration
Data Collection Sheet” for each blackbody temperature. This simulates various source Irradiance
levels covering the operating range. To best align with the test procedures, a unique “Radiometer
Calibration Data Collection Sheet” is used for each temperature and radiometer.
Table III shows the test matrix for the calibration of the two radiometers. Each radiometer is tested
separately, and aligned normal to the blackbody source. The output voltage is recorded at each
temperature and aperture value in the table. To gain some redundancy in the calibration data, the test
matrix spans the envelope of the minimum and maximum required irradiance values, as documented
in FLX-REQ-0001, and indicated in TABLE III.

5.1.2 FOV Roll-off Characterization
The instrument function of the radiometer package is measured over a range of off-axis alignment for
each radiometer. As the neutral mid-point, each radiometer is centered and aligned normal to the
blackbody source, at a distance of 11.0 cm from the blackbody aperture to the radiometer TO-5 can
face. The radiometer is translated in the horizontal (X) direction over a range of +/- 70 mm about this
center, at 10 mm increments, while recording the output signal level. The transverse off-axis
characterization is measured by translating the blackbody source on a lab jack from +/- 65 mm to
measure the Y roll-off characteristics, while the X axis is at the center point. The Field of View
Characterization Procedure (APPENDIX D) and FOV Characterization Data Collection Sheet
(APPENDIX E) are used to implement this characterization.
5.1.3 Signal to Noise Ratio Characterization
The signal-to-noise characteristics of the radiometers are measured at minimum signal level, medium
signal level, and high signal level. The time sequence of samples is measured by an oscilloscope
sampling AC and DC at 25 kHz. The DC input is the signal, and the AC input is the noise in the
sampling bandwidth. The AC sampling is smoothed over 10 milliseconds to represent the flight
acquisition sample time. Data are logged on the SNR Data Collection Sheet (APPENDIX F).
5.1.4 Response Time Characterization
The response time of the narrowband and broadband detectors are measured using the calibrated
blackbody source with a chopper wheel to provide a step function illumination input at a frequency of
2Hz. The output voltage is analyzed to calculate the rise time from 0 to 62.5% of the maximum
signal response.
5.1.5 Thermal Stability
The stability of the radiometer over the working range of ambient temperatures is observed by
soaking the radiometers and blackbody source in a thermal chamber set from 20 to 30 degrees
Celsius.
5.2 Data Collection and Reporting
All data are collected and recorded on the attached data sheets. Data sheets will be maintained to
document the history of the FLEX-2 Radiometer Calibration. The data sheets include, but are not
limited to, the following information:
1. Date and time
2. Identity of individual making the entry
3. Environmental conditions
4. Performance parameter measurements
5. Power ”On” Time
6. Failure observations
7. Configuration identification
8. Record of non-conformances, repair / maintenance actions, etc

6.1 Radiometric Calibration
The sections below show the results of the calibrations using the shielded breadboard configuration

The accuracy requirement per FLX-REQ-0001 4.1.79 is 5% from minimum to maximum irradiance.

The equation of the fit with slope, intercept, and correlation coefficient are shown.
The figure shows the data independent of the aperture/temperature combination used to achieve the
irradiance values, so some as-yet uncorrected systematic error(s) presumably tend to spread the data.

6.2 Field of View (FOV) Roll-Off Measurement or Instrument Function
The roll-off in response was measured to simulate off-axis readings of droplets. The off-axis position
of a droplet on orbit is assumed to be determined using the imaging cameras. Given said position, the
radiometric response can be scaled to the full on-axis calibration curves.
The procedures outlined in MDC-TST-1866 were followed and data documented on the data sheets.
The results are summarized below. The experimental setup is shown in FIGURE 5 and FIGURE 8,
configured without a radiation shield.

6.2.1 Broadband
The broadband radiometer response to off-axis translations is given in FIGURE 13. It shows the X
(horizontal in the figures, along the axis parallel to the line bisecting the radiometer apertures) and Y
(vertical in the figures, along the axis perpendicular to the line bisecting the radiometer apertures)
roll-off. Prior to the measurements the radiometer was aligned to the blackbody source, so as to peak
the signal output.
During the scan, the center of symmetry does not completely agree with the peaked position, as
indicated by the X and Y fits of -0.6 mm and 1.2 mm, respectively. These centers were
center center
calculated by determining the full width half maximum (FWHM) points on each curve and
interpolating to get the position of each FWHM point. TABLE VI shows the data for the centers and
field of view (FOV) calculations. The 10% roll-off point was used to verify the alignment of the
radiometer to the measurement location, and the 90% roll-off point was used to determine the overall
FOV.

6.5 Ambient Temperature Dependence
The thermopile detectors used in the FLEX-2 radiometers are relatively insensitive to signal change
as a function of ambient temperature. The radiometer output was tested over the ambient temperature
range expected on-orbit, from 20 to 30 °C, with the setup in the thermal chamber as shown in

FIGURE 20 shows voltage readings of the narrowband radiometer in blue and of the broadband
radiometer in red at ambient temperatures of 30, 25, and 20 °C. There are no trends in voltage
proportional to ambient temperature, but it is hard to judge if the variation in output is significant
relative to the system noise. To this end, the random noise and drift are shown in FIGURE 21, and
the two data sets are superposed with the same voltage scale (but offset) in FIGURE 22. FIGURE 22
then makes it clear that both the broadband and narrowband radiometer variations in the thermal
chamber are of the same magnitude as the noise and drift.

filtered irradiance values that better represent the voltage outputs. The filtered irradiance is different
for each blackbody temperature irradiating the detector, and is given by the calculated fractional
irradiance plot provided by the Project Scientist in FIGURE 11. The corrected narrowband
radiometer’s calibration curve, shown in FIGURE 12, improves the slope error to agree well with the
